# Diagnosing No-Crank and Flicker Symptoms in a 2007 Hyundai Entourage

When a vehicle exhibits no noise upon turning the ignition key while interior lights flicker, you are looking at a classic high-resistance ground or weak battery scenario rather than an alternator failure. The fact that the starter motor receives power (enough to light up the dashboard) but lacks the current required to overcome its internal resistance and engage the flywheel indicates a bottleneck in the circuit. Since your alternator was replaced two months ago, we can reasonably exclude the charging system as the primary culprit for a recurring no-crank condition, assuming it has passed a basic load test.

The flickering interior lights are the tell-tale sign here. When you turn the key to "Start," the starter solenoid attempts to draw hundreds of amps from the battery. If the main ground connection is corroded or loose at the chassis battery terminal or the engine block, the voltage drops across that resistance spike. This voltage sag causes the accessory circuits powered by a separate fuse tap or a less robust ground path (like interior lights) to momentarily dip below their operating threshold, resulting in a flicker before the system resets. In a 2007 Hyundai Entourage, this often manifests as a corroded negative terminal clamp that has oxidized over time or a loose engine-to-chassis ground strap.

To isolate the issue systematically, you need to verify battery voltage under load versus open-circuit voltage. With a digital multimeter in hand, measure the voltage at the battery terminals with the engine off. A healthy 12V lead-acid battery should read between 12.4V and 12.7V. However, this static measurement tells you nothing about health under stress. Attempt to crank the engine while monitoring the voltage at the battery posts. If the reading drops below 9.6V during the attempt, the battery is incapable of delivering sufficient current, or there is excessive resistance in the path.

If the battery tests good and the voltage drop occurs only when cranking, focus on the ground straps. On this model year, locate the negative battery cable connection at the chassis and the ground strap running from the engine block to the frame. Disconnect these connections one by one while monitoring for a significant voltage difference between the battery negative post and the engine block with the key in the "Run" position (ignition on, no crank). A reading greater than 0.1V indicates resistance in that specific path. Clean the terminals with a wire brush until bare metal is exposed, apply dielectric grease to prevent future oxidation, and re-tighten to specification.

Another potential pitfall involves the starter solenoid itself. Even if it clicks or hums faintly (which you noted as "no noise," suggesting no engagement at all), the contacts inside can be pitted or burned, creating a high-resistance junction that limits current flow enough to flicker lights but not enough to spin the engine. If cleaning grounds yields no improvement and the battery is confirmed healthy, swapping the starter assembly with a known good unit is often more cost-effective than rebuilding it, given the labor involved in removing the transmission or subframe on an Entourage.

Finally, verify that the ignition switch is mechanically engaging the starter circuit properly. While less common to cause flickering lights specifically, a worn switch can interrupt power intermittently. If all electrical paths are clean and voltage delivery is confirmed, the issue lies within the starter assembly's internal contacts or the solenoid mechanism. Always ensure you have charged the battery immediately after a jump-start attempt to avoid introducing further corrosion from acid leakage during a failed start cycle.
